description: Somos un equipo interdisciplinario de seis estudiantes de la Universidad Pontificia Bolivariana, conformado por tres estudiantes de Ingeniería Aeronáutica y tres de Ingeniería de Sistemas. Integramos conocimientos de ingeniería, tecnología, programación, análisis de datos e innovación para abordar desafíos reales y desarrollar soluciones con impacto, representando el talento y compromiso de nuestra Universidad.
summary:
NASA’s Earth Information Center shows our planet through striking images, but images speak only to those who can see them. Earth Jukebox turns that science into sound to give the Amazon a voice: the lungs of the world, home to the richest biodiversity on Earth, and a forest Colombia shares.
We built an immersive experience on an interactive 3D Earth where four NASA datasets each have their own voice. Forest height measured by GEDI sounds as a higher, fuller note. Wildfire smoke from MERRA-2 makes the sound rough and dark. Carbon dioxide from OCO-2 GEOS beats like a breath that quickens. Lightning seen from the International Space Station answers with thunder. Latitude, longitude and time shape pitch, panning and volume: as the globe turns, the sound travels from one ear to the other, and a double-click flies you into the Amazon to hear how a single place changes over time.
Earth Jukebox opens Earth science to people who are blind or have low vision, to those who learn by listening, and to anyone who has never heard their planet breathe.
details:
Earth Jukebox is a web application that lets you listen to different components of the Earth. It opens onto a 3D planet. Because browsers keep audio muted until the user enables it, the experience begins when you click Start sound and choose one of the four layers. The sound follows the visible portion of the Earth, with lower notes toward the poles and higher ones toward the equator, while stereo panning moves it from left to right as the globe rotates, allowing you to hear its position as well. Double-clicking on a region, or clicking the Amazon button, centers the globe on a detailed regional map. There, a click locks the sound onto a specific point, dragging reveals how values shift from one place to another, and a timeline with play, pause, and speed controls lets you hear how a single location changes over time. The “?” button opens a tutorial explaining every control. In addition, five soundscapes across the Amazon—each featuring a photograph, a brief explanation, and a field recording—highlight both its natural richness and the impact of deforestation.

Each layer has its own timbre and musical scale, and only the selected layer plays at any given time. In the globe view, the entire visible field is sonified across a 12 × 12 grid: on-screen position determines panning, latitude determines pitch, and the data value controls volume, using a threshold relative to the average of what is currently in view. On the regional map, you listen to a single point: its left-to-right position sets the panning, and the layer's value triggers a discrete note within a one-octave range of its scale. The voice is enriched with detuning, sub-octave harmonics, chorus, reverb, and air or bird textures depending on the chosen layer.

Forest height, measured by GEDI between 2019 and 2025 on a scale from 0 to 50 m, serves as the static reference layer and shapes the regions. Smoke, from MERRA-2, with three-hourly data between August and September 2026, uses a suspended pentatonic scale layered with an air texture. CO₂, from OCO-2 GEOS, featuring daily data from 2020 on a scale from 404 to 420 ppm, uses a minor pentatonic scale, also with an air texture. Lightning, from the LIS instrument, with monthly data between 2017 and 2023, plays as percussive notes with decay at a tempo between 90 and 120 bpm.

The first benefit is accessibility. Earth science that exists solely as visual imagery excludes blind and low-vision people, and sound opens a door for them. It also helps sighted users: hearing a value while looking at it deepens understanding, makes temporal patterns easier to spot—storms rising and falling with the seasons, carbon dioxide climbing over the course of the year, plumes of smoke drifting out over the ocean—and turns a static image into something you actively explore. Because it runs in any modern browser, it can easily reach classrooms, museums, and communities.

The impact we seek is comprehension. We want people to understand the Amazon as a living system: the forest is its foundation, wildfire smoke threatens it, atmospheric carbon provides the global context that makes protecting it urgent, and storms are part of the water cycle that sustains it. For the SAGITTA team, based in Medellín, this is not some distant forest—it is a territory that Colombia shares. Our next steps unfold in three stages. First, we will test with diverse listeners to understand what sensations the sound evokes. Next, we will evaluate the complete experience, bringing visuals and timbres together to ensure it conveys what we intend. Finally, we will conduct user testing with blind and low-vision participants until we achieve full accessibility support that allows them to explore the sound of a place like a melody.

The data pipeline, written in Rust, converts NASA datasets into global grids of up to 1440 × 720 cells, a finer-resolution grid for the Amazon, textures, and a manifest containing sources, scales, and dates. The interface is built with React, Tailwind, GSAP, and three.js, while the Web Audio API synthesizes sound in real time, interpolating both spatially and across dates. A Rust server powered by Axum serves the application. Docker allows it to run offline, and the live version is hosted at https://www.earthjukebox.tech/. Testing is handled with Vitest and Rust, and Natural Earth provides the base map, which contains no data layers.

Earth Jukebox treats each dataset as an instrument in an ensemble rather than a graph read aloud. The listener does not hear numbers; they hear the forest, the air turning harsh with smoke, the planet breathing faster, and storms rumbling in the distance. Space becomes sound through stereo panning, and time becomes rhythm through the timeline. The journey from the whole planet down to a specific region is a movement the user controls, or an experience that envelops them. The soundscapes add another dimension: water, rain, wildlife, and wind weave into a composition that stirs emotion, sparks the imagination, and reveals the richness of nature. Each sound carries its own meaning and, blending with the others, creates an atmosphere that invites you to listen, explore, and understand the world through your senses. In this way, Earth Jukebox invites you to explore the Earth just as you would explore a song.

With this in mind, our core values center on scientific honesty: every layer uses a fixed scale, and every value is described for what it truly is—whether a satellite measurement, a model estimate, or a relative frequency read from a visualization. Carbon dioxide is presented as global context rather than a localized effect measured within the Amazon, and each layer preserves its own distinct timeframe. We also balance scientific fidelity with listenability, using pentatonic scales and soft textures so people want to keep listening. Above all, we design for clarity, featuring a single voice at a time and a guided walkthrough.
